opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm not a VC myself, so take this as an outsider's view, though I've talked with quite a few investors over the past couple of years.

For a research team, especially in AI right now, I think the first thing they look at is the people. Early on there's usually no product, no revenue, sometimes not even a clear market, so the bet is really on whether the team can do something other people can't. They look at track record: have these people actually built things that worked, published work that changed how the field thinks, or shipped systems at scale? A paper count by itself doesn't mean much. What matters is whether the work had real impact, and whether the team has the taste to pick the right problems.

The second thing is whether there's a believable story connecting the research to something valuable. Investors don't need you to have the product figured out, but they want to see that if the research succeeds, there's a path to a big outcome. A lot of research teams struggle here. Researchers tend to talk about what's interesting, and VCs want to hear about what's important and what could be defensible. Those overlap, but they're not the same.

Third, timing and the broader narrative matter a lot, maybe more than people admit. When a field is hot, as large models have been, capital flows toward teams that fit the current story. A strong team working on something the market doesn't yet believe in can have a much harder time than a weaker team riding the wave. So part of the decision is really a bet on where the consensus is going.

There's also a practical side. Research is expensive now. If you need large amounts of compute, investors have to believe you can turn that spending into something before the money runs out, and that bigger players won't simply do it first. "Why you, and why won't Google or OpenAI just do this?" comes up a lot.

So it's a mix of judging people, judging the vision, and judging timing. Since the outcomes are so uncertain, I think many VCs lean on pattern-matching and on signals from other trusted people. That works reasonably well, but it also means truly unconventional research directions often get overlooked at first.

r001.rationale: The response says investors look first at the people and that, early on, the investment is a bet on whether the team can do what others cannot.

r002.rationale: It discusses track record and research impact as factors in evaluating a team, but does not state that later funding depends on progress the team demonstrates.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think most VCs don't fund research teams in the traditional sense. They fund people and a story. If you look at who got money in the last couple of years, it's not that an investor read the papers and evaluated the technical contribution. It's that they looked at the track record of the founders, where they came from, what they built before, and whether those people have a credible shot at turning a research direction into a product on a timeline that matters.

So there are a few things they actually look at. First, pedigree and signal: did this team ship something that mattered, like a model or a system that other people use? Second, is there a thesis about why now, why this group can do something the big labs can't or won't? And third, whether the team can execute. A lot of researchers are great at exploring, but a company requires converging. Investors try to read whether you can make that switch.

From my own experience doing research for a long time, I'd say there is a gap between what makes good research and what makes a fundable company. Good research is about open questions and taking risks on ideas that might not work. A startup needs a direction where the risk is in execution, not in whether the science is real. The teams that raise well are usually the ones that have already de-risked the science and can show a clear path from the idea to something people pay for. If you're still in the "we think this might work" phase, that's a grant, not a venture round.

r001.rationale: The response says VCs fund people and a story, emphasizing founders’ track records, prior work, and ability to execute. This conveys that funding is primarily grounded in confidence in the team.

r002.rationale: The response mentions prior accomplishments and de-risked science as factors in raising, but does not state that subsequent funding depends on progress demonstrated after an initial investment.

astra-6.text:
I think venture capitalists are trying to understand whether a research advantage can become a business advantage. A team might have a very impressive paper, but investors will ask: What does this enable? Who needs it badly enough to pay for it? And why is this team better positioned than anyone else to deliver it?

At an early stage, there may not be enough evidence to answer all of those questions, so the people matter a lot. Can they explain their insight clearly? Can they execute? And can they adapt when an experiment fails or a customer wants something different from what they originally imagined?

There’s also a question of timing. A research direction could be valuable eventually, but it might require more time and capital than a particular fund can commit. So a decision not to invest doesn’t necessarily mean the research is bad. It may mean the investor doesn’t see a sufficiently clear path from the research to a product within their investment horizon.

r001.rationale: The response says people matter a lot at an early stage and asks about their abilities, but it does not state that initial funding is based primarily on investors’ trust in the team.

r002.rationale: The response discusses evidence available at an early stage, but does not say that subsequent funding depends on the progress the team demonstrates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think venture capitalists are trying to answer a few questions: Is this team working on an important problem? Do they have an advantage that’s difficult for others to replicate? And can that advantage eventually turn into a business?

For a research team, the challenge is that a promising research direction doesn’t necessarily come with a clear product or timeline. So investors look at the people: their track record, how deeply they understand the problem, and whether they can adapt when an approach doesn’t work. They also want to see some evidence—a prototype, an experimental result, or customer interest—that connects the research to something people will actually use.

Different investors will weigh those things differently. Some are comfortable taking a long-term bet on the team; others need a much clearer path to revenue.

r001.rationale: The response says investors consider the team’s track record and ability, but does not state that initial funding is based primarily on trust in the people.

r002.rationale: It mentions evidence such as prototypes or experimental results, but does not connect demonstrated progress to subsequent funding.
